catalog_quote: There are no accentless words in Hamar, and there is only one prominent syllable per word, cued by high pitch, loudness and increased duration. ... Hamar has two co-existing, yet independent systems which can be analysed in terms of stress and tone. ... Stress in nouns is lexical and its position is not predictable. In disyllabic nouns, either the final or the penultimate syllable can be stressed. In disyllabic nouns composed of a heavy syllable, stress is attested in any position: shaa.lá ‘ceiling’ zíi.ga ‘spinal cord’ síl.qa ‘knuckle’ gur.dá ‘village’ Stress in nouns can be lexically distinctive. A few σ́σ vs. σσ́ minimal pairs occurring in the same grammatical domain have been attested: ... átti ʻbirdʼ attí ʻfermented sorghum’ ... Trisyllabic nouns can have a final, penultimate or antepenultimate stressed syllable as displayed in the CV.CV.CV minimal pairs below. ánqasi ‘bee’ anqási …

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: every fragment of the deciding quotation, the domain quote and the exceptions quote is verbatim in the held extracted text of Petrollino 2016 at the recorded pages (pp. 40-42, 47, 49-52); locator correct after the stage-C fix. (2) Deciding source: a 2016 fieldwork reference grammar (Leiden PhD = Köppe Cushitic and Omotic Studies 6, confirmed on the Leiden repository record), Glottolog's top and only 'grammar' entry, with an instrumented prosody section; it is the best available description. (3) The one additional dedicated prosody study, Petrollino 2019 (LangSci, open access), was fetched sources to and read: it restates that accent is obligatory, culminative, weight-insensitive and 'lexically contrastive in any word position in nouns', grammatical in verbs, with tone-like H/HL contrasts confined to verbal suffixes and masculine-noun

sources.citation: Petrollino, Sara. 2019. Between tone and stress in Hamar. In Emily Clem, Peter Jenks & Hannah Sande (eds.), Theory and description in African Linguistics: Selected papers from the 47th Annual Conference on African Linguistics (Contemporary African Linguistics 4), 287-302. Berlin: Language Science Press. DOI 10.5281/zenodo.3367150.
sources.quote: p. 293: 'Accented syllables in both nouns and verbs are obligatory and culminative (19). These properties, together with the fact that the syllable, rather than the mora, is the TBU (20), correspond to the definitional characteristics of stress accent (Hyman 2006: 231).' p. 294: 'The position of the accent is not sensitive to syllable weight: the heavy syllables CVV and CVC in the bisyllabic words in (21) do not always attract accent. ... In trisyllabic nouns accent is found on the antepenultimate, penultimate and final syllable ... Accent in nouns is thus unpredictable and lexically distincti
